headline.main: Skeletons Emerging from the Closet: Deutsche Bank CEO Sewing Facing Questions as Lawsuits Loom
headline.social: Skeletons Emerging from the Closet: Deutsche Bank CEO Sewing Facing Questions as Lawsuits Loom

intro: Christian Sewing has steered Deutsche Bank back onto the right track and restored its reputation. But now, a scandal from the financial crisis is returning to haunt him.
text:
Christian Sewing’s career could hardly be more upstanding. It is one that has seen him rise to very top of the banking world despite his rather milquetoast persona. And he has done so at Deutsche Bank of all places, a financial institution that has been no stranger to scandal in recent years – and which is home to all manner of banking prodigies and inflated egos.
In the span of 36 years, Sewing has gone from being a trainee in Bielefeld to the CEO’s office of Germany’s largest bank, a seat he has managed to hold on to for quite a bit longer than a number of his predecessors. The man with an aura of a rock-solid home-grown talent has managed to achieve the apparently impossible: Freeing Deutsche Bank from its image as a hotbed of scandal and bringing it back to its roots as a profit-making machine.
This year alone, the bank’s stock price has already jumped by 51 percent. The contrast to his early days couldn’t be starker, a time when he found himself facing a series of scandals, billions in fines and internal strife.
Sewing, 55 years old, annual salary of 9.8 million euros, is at the apex of his career.
But at precisely this moment, the past has caught up to Sewing and he finds himself in a position where he must explain himself. His reputation is at stake: Did he take care of the dirty work for others to wash them clean of a financial scandal?
At issue are complex derivative deals made with the bank Monte dei Paschi di Siena in the financial crisis year of 2008 that are now casting a shadow over Frankfurt-based Deutsche Bank. Balance-sheet shenanigans under the name "Santorini,” an angry regulatory official, a mysterious death and internal inconsistencies in which Sewing played a key role.
Dario Schiraldi, the former head of the Deutsche Bank division dealing with the institution’s largest clients and once one of the bank’s top earners, has filed a suit against his former employer in the regional court in Frankfurt. He is demanding unpaid wages and bonuses amounting to at least 152 million euros. Oral arguments are to take place on December 4. DER SPIEGEL has obtained the statement of claim and numerous additional documents (Az. 2-19 O 153/24). Schiraldi did not respond to DER SPIEGEL attempts to contact him.
A handful of other former employees have also threatened to file suit, though in English courts. One of those is Michele Faissola, a wiry Italian from Liguria who was the long-time head of the global interest rate department in addition to being a member of the board and a close confidant of former Deutsche Bank CEO Anshuman Jain, the investment banking legend who died in 2022. When added together, the lawsuits could easily amount to a total well into the three-figure millions.
The dubious banking practices are well known. They resulted in Schiraldi and others being sentenced to several years behind bars in a 2019 trial in Milan before an appeals court exonerated them in 2022. Thus far, though, the dirty deals have been seen as schemes perpetrated by individuals, testing the limits without informing bank management.
That interpretation, though, could now shift. Schiraldi and the other potential plaintiffs don’t just want money. More than anything, they finally want to wash themselves clean of accusations that they acted on their own against the interests of the bank.
They are demanding recompense, maybe even revenge. Faissola, in particular, is primarily focused on rehabilitation, say those close to him, since he’s already got enough money.
According to Schiraldi’s lawsuit, the most important members of the management and supervisory boards had actually known about the deals with Monte dei Paschi. The lawsuit also claims that Sewing, head of the internal auditing department (Group Audit) at the time, deceived the regulatory authorities on the instructions of his superiors to incriminate the plaintiffs who are now filing suit.
Due to the "aggressive scrutiny of their balance sheet by regulators,” reads the 154-page-long complaint, Deutsche Bank and its leaders felt their "financial integrity” was in danger. For that reason, they turned to "desperate and criminal measures” to "ensure the survival of the bank and divert attention from failures in management.”
They are serious accusations against the bank and its former executives, and against the present-day CEO, who is mentioned by name on several pages. The complaint portrays Sewing as a willing accomplice to the bank’s management at the time. As someone who did what was asked of him despite his obligation to maintain a critical distance as the bank’s chief auditor.
Sewing, in short, plays a central role in the complaint – in part, perhaps, to maximize the damage done to the bank’s reputation and, thus, maximize the sum of money the plaintiffs can demand. Deutsche Bank considers the lawsuit to be unfounded. It is, the bank says, based on "incorrect claims against the details of which the bank has defended itself in court and will continue to do so.” Schiraldi, the bank claims, was largely responsible for the "Santorini transaction,” which led to considerable reputational and financial risks for Deutsche Bank.
A full understanding of the case requires a trip back in time to the years prior to and immediately following the financial crisis. It was an era when Deutsche Bank was led by Josef Ackermann, a Swiss national who had high expectations when it came to profitability and investment returns. Back then, the bank Ackermann ran was seen as a potential European challenger to the titans of Wall Street, thanks to hard-nosed traders like Jain, Faissola and others. Sewing was not among them. He was pursuing a career as an auditor and risk manager at the time.
Traders pursue their trades with plenty of ambition, but not much capital. From a financial point of view, this makes a lot of sense. After all, high turnover and low equity translates into a high return on equity. And back then, that was the most important criterion for global financial institutions, particularly investment banks. Ackermann set a goal of 25 percent return on equity.
To achieve that target, his traders took huge risks – for the bank and for the bank’s customers. With little capital, they made huge deals and earned billions. For a time, Deutsche Bank was seen as the most dangerous bank in the world, as little more than a hedge fund with a banking license. It is a reputation the bank has never managed to fully shed. In the financial crisis, after the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy, Deutsche Bank looked for a time as though it might be the next domino to fall.
But things hadn’t advanced that far in 2007, when Deutsche Bank began trying to push a new financial product on its customers called "repo-to-maturity.” It sounds complicated, and the details are indeed confusing, but essentially, it follows a simple principle: Bank A sells securities, usually government bonds, to Bank B. Bank B wires the nominal value of the securities, cash, to Bank A. Once the deal comes to an end, Bank A receives its bonds back while the cash is returned to Bank B.
It's a good deal for both sides. A can use the money it receives from B to plug holes in its balance sheet, invest or do other things. B, meanwhile, earns money from the commission that A pays for the transaction to be concluded in the first place.
Essentially, repo deals are like loans guaranteed using securities. With a crucial difference: Normally when banks make loans, they must reserve equity on their balance sheets, which makes it easier to absorb losses should those loans default.
But in the case of repo deals, the institution making the loan is able to offset the opposing positions – bonds for cash – against each other. Experts refer to the practice as "netting.” The result is a deal in which billions in cash and securities change hands, but the total on paper is tiny – and doesn’t have to be backed by equity. The risks of the transactions disappear on the balance sheet. And if all goes well, both sides earn money.
At that time, such deals looked extremely attractive to Deutsche Bank because the bank was short on equity. And because large deals presumably carrying little risk produce significant profits. In 2007, Deutsche Bank closed around 100 repo deals with a variety of different clients, including foreign banks, the French railway, Spanish supermarkets and others. They are included in the complaint that Schiraldi submitted to the court in Frankfurt. The cumulative volume of the deals: an unimaginable 35 billion euros – all without having to dedicate valuable equity, which was in short supply anyway. That equity was thus freed up to be used elsewhere.
Repo transactions were the new big thing for the investment bankers surrounding Faissola, Schiraldi and the other plaintiffs. But Sewing played a key role in his position as auditor and risk manager.
In the key year of 2008, Banca Monte dei Paschi from the Tuscany region of Italy was in bad shape. It’s investment in the Italian rival bank Intesa Sanpaolo from Turin had proven to be a disaster, and the steep downward trajectory of the company’s stock price showed no signs of reversal. Losses from the investment, parked at a subsidiary called Santorini, climbed to more than 300 million euros. The price for Monte dei Paschi shares was also in freefall. The world’s oldest bank, founded in 1472, was on the verge of collapse.
The financial alchemists from Deutsche Bank were a welcome sight. In December 2008, they offered Monte dei Paschi a repo transaction in which the Sienna-based bank would give the Germans Italian sovereign bonds worth 2 billion euros and would receive 364 million euros in cash in exchange – just before the balance sheet closed at the end of the year. The transaction was set to be unwound several years later, meaning Monte dei Paschi was saved for the time being.
The Santorini deal – the name likely derives from the words Sanpaolo, Torino and the Greek island of Santorini – wasn’t per se forbidden. It was, however, extremely problematic because of the lack of clarity it imparted to the balance sheets of both banks. After the Lehmann Brothers collapse in 2008 and revelations about its rather creative accounting practices, both the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Reserve had begun to view repo transactions with a fair degree of suspicion.
But Monte dei Paschi and Deutsche Bank didn’t seem to care. The Italian bank was able to conceal its losses and the Germans were able to make a loan without having to devote any equity to cover default risk. Sovereign bonds, though – particularly Italian – can represent a significant risk, as would become clear during the European debt crisis that would soon begin to unfold.
The deal went unnoticed until Monte dei Paschi did finally collapse in 2011 due to other missteps. That same year, the American derivative broker MF Global went bankrupt due to repo agreements, leading the SEC and the Fed to exert even more leverage on internationally active banks to improve transparency.
They wanted to know how much gross risk the financial institutions were carrying on their balance sheets – and not just the much smaller totals listed through the practice of netting as described above. For regulatory authorities seeking to determine how stable a bank was, the artificially minimized risk presented through netting was an impenetrable veil.
And it was soon to become illegal. Global regulators decided that as of 2014, the practice of netting in transactions like the Santorini deal would be banned. The vast majority of banks immediately took steps to comply, either by increasing their equity or completely backing away from repo agreements altogether.
In 2011, Deutsche Bank also had three years to comply. But instead, the Germans opted in fall 2013 for a balance sheet trick: They simply retroactively reclassified the Santorini deal – and many other repo transactions – on their balance sheet as a derivative deal instead of a credit transaction. For such deals, netting was still allowed. While it may sound complicated, it is actually quite simple: The old trick simply was simply given a new name.
Executives were well aware that Deutsche Bank, by doing so, was deviating from standard industry practice. That is made clear by an October 2009 email exchange between members of the finance department and the accounting department. "KMPG (the auditing firm) and APAG (Accounting Policy Group – Deutsche Bank’s accounting department) have asked around and no one else is using the netting route, so although that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t either, it makes them a little uncomfortable. They are unclear after netting what remains on the B/S (balance sheet) to evidence any residual exposure, what risk is left in financial statements."
In practice, reclassifying the Santorini deal wasn’t so simple. To make a restatement, as such balance sheet corrections are called, the bank had to submit a convincing explanation to the supervisory authorities. But Deutsche Bank had one prepared.
In 2013, Deutsche Bank told financial regulators that it had only just learned an important fact. The Santorini team, the bank insisted, had failed to disclose the loan nature of the 2008 deal to top management. Schiraldi and the others, the bank insisted, hadn’t passed along the information internally that the sovereign bonds delivered by Monte dei Paschi to Deutsche Bank in exchange for cash hadn’t actually been purchased by the Italians on the open market, but had come from Deutsche Bank via an intermediary. As such, Faissola and his people had knowingly assisted Monte dei Paschi in cooking its books.
This discovery, and not the new balance sheet regulations, made a restatement of the repo agreement necessary – such was the bank’s narrative according to the lawsuit. Officially, the bank’s explanation reads: "In processing this transaction, Deutsche Bank adhered to applicable laws and regulations, including international accounting standards. This was confirmed by internal and external audits. The bank did not derive any material financial or accounting benefit from the restatement.”
The entire lawsuit now hinges entirely on this restatement. As does Sewing’s reputation.
The plaintiffs consider the bank’s justification to be merely a pretense. With the restatement, according to the lawsuit, bank executives just wanted to take the bank out of the regulatory firing line and deflect attention from the fact that top managers were well aware of the circumstances surrounding the Santorini deal, including how the sovereign bonds were procured, and that they knew about the originally, rather dubious accounting.
The lawsuit claims that the Santorini deal was actually orchestrated by then-board members Stefan Krause (finance), Stefan Leithner (legal) and Christian Sewing (chief auditor). Supervisory Board Chair Paul Achleitner was also allegedly in the know.
The bank rejects the claim. It argues that it consistently behaved in an upstanding manner, sacrificed nobody and even spent millions of euros to defend Schiraldi, Faissola and the others in the Italian criminal case and protecting their interests. Schiraldi was given a severance payment when he left the company by mutual agreement in 2016, the bank says, and he waived all claims against Deutsche Bank. Krause, Leithner, Achleitner, Sewing and Faissola have all declined comment.
Plaintiff Schiraldi claims that top management tried to dress up the story of the Santorini team’s alleged sole responsibility in a respectable guise. To this end, CFO Krause commissioned Sewing, the chief auditor, with a special investigation. On November 13, 2013, Krause emailed Sewing: "I was tasked to ask you to get on this immediately."
The problem, according to the lawsuit, is that the result of the special investigation had already been decided upon before it was even launched. Krause, the lawsuit alleges, had specified the objectives and scope of the investigation, meaning that its results were clear from the outset.
Instead of investigating whether a restatement was even necessary, the lawsuit claims, Sewing’s people focused on demonstrating that the Santorini team had withheld information, thus making the balance sheet correction unavoidable.
On top of that, the lawsuit notes, Krause’s finance department should have been a focus of the audit rather than commissioning it in the first place, since it was responsible for the accounting on the Santorini deal. That view was also taken by the appeals court in Milan, which exonerated Faissola, Schiraldi and the others in October 2022.
Deutsche Bank, for its part, argues that Krause in no way set the objectives of the investigation. The defense statement rejects the plaintiff’s assertion that Sewing produced the result desired by the bank. "The internal investigation was conducted thoroughly, properly and independently, and the managers involved fulfilled all of their responsibilities in an appropriate manner,” the bank says. Deutsche Bank also notes in its counterargument that an expert opinion produced by the auditing firm PSP on behalf of the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin) found no evidence of impropriety or manipulation. Instead, the statement continues, Sewing’s investigation uncovered "significant failings in the handling of the transactions, both by the team that made the deal and in other departments. This included the failure to disclose sufficient information to ensure proper review of the transactions before they were executed.”
It is, in other words, as it always is with lawsuits of this size: The two sides, armed with evaluations and investigations, are exchanging accusations and counter-accusations.
The special investigation was followed by disciplinary proceedings resulting in sanctions against Schiraldi and others. Faissola, a close confidant of Jain’s, was initially spared.
Viewed from the outside, it is rather remarkable just how perfectly the results of Sewing’s investigation matched up with what benefited the bank’s top executives: The accounting of their multi-billion-euro repo transaction was not fundamentally called into question and Santorini was portrayed as a misstep, with blame falling on the shoulders of Faissola, Schiraldi and co.
And the internal investigation wasn’t the end of it. Sewing’s representatives sent the results of the audit and of the disciplinary proceedings to Italy’s central bank, the Banca d’Italia, which has oversight over the country’s financial institutions. The lawsuit accuses Deutsche Bank of suggesting to the Italians that Schiraldi and his colleagues had engaged in market manipulation in order to help Monte dei Paschi cook its books. Schiraldi’s lawyers now say that the Italian authorities were thus compelled to bring charges against the Santorini team.
And Schiraldi’s legal team allege that Deutsche Bank’s interactions with the Italian authorities sank to even more sinister depths. The plaintiff brief claims that Schiraldi had been exonerated by an internal appeals panel, but that Deutsche Bank did not pass that information along to the Italians, even though the management board had been informed.
Deutsche Bank counters by saying it is "completely implausible to claim that the bank had intentionally provoked criminal proceedings of which it was also a target. We as Deutsche Bank also faced serious allegations from Italian prosecutors and were found liable by the court of first instance.”
The lawsuit, though, claims that Deutsche Bank also sought to protect its interests in the Italian court proceedings against the Santorini team. The Germans allegedly provided support to the Santorini defendants in the person of tax expert Michele Caso, who was involved in formulating the 2013 restatement – the reclassification of the Santorini deal on Deutsche Bank’s balance sheet – in the hopes of saving the bank a lot of trouble from the supervisory authorities. Schiraldi and the others apparently knew nothing of this conflict of interest. The bank did not provide comment on the claim.
And Sewing? The Schiraldi lawsuit claims that the chief auditor had defended the results of his internal investigation to BaFin – despite the bank’s own appeals panel having come to the conclusion that "key findings” of the audit "were incorrect.”
A report from the auditing firm Grant Thornton likewise delivers a harsh verdict on the work of Deutsche Bank’s current CEO. Grant Thornton launched its own evaluation of the case in 2020 at the behest of one of the Santorini team members following the initial guilty verdict in the first instance.
In its report, Grant Thornton accuses Deutsche Bank of improprieties in its handling of the case and of suppressing important evidence. Consequently, the court of appeals in Milan reversed the lower court verdict, and documented the questionable conduct of Deutsche Bank in doing so. The Corte Suprema di Cassazione, Italy’s highest court, confirmed the verdict in 2023.
Shady risk transactions that top executives are said to have known about in 2008; an allegedly manipulated report to absolve management of any responsibility; the deliberate sacrifice of the Santorini team: The accusations made by Schiraldi’s lawyers cannot be taken lightly.
And there might be something to them. There is an email from December 2008 that appears to counter claims by Deutsche Bank that the Santorini team acted on its own. The email was from William Broeksmit, a risk manager who enjoyed a significant amount of respect within the company, to a colleague who had described the Santorini deal to him and pointed out the possible risks: "I think this should be presented to Anshu.”
Anshu is Anshuman Jain, leader at the time of the global capital markets department and one of the most important men in the entire company. A "rainmaker,” whose traders, known internally as "Anshu’s army,” were earning billions for the bank at the time.
It is unclear whether Broeksmit’s warning about the Santorini deal ever reached Jain. But how likely is it that Deutsche Bank’s top investment banker knew nothing of his foot soldiers seeking to sell a client like Monte dei Paschi a potentially immensely profitable product that also provides protection to a balance sheet weak on capital? Particularly when Broeksmit, with whom he worked closely, was warning of "reputational risks” associated with Santorini?
Jain became Deutsche Bank co-CEO in 2012 together with executive Jürgen Fitschen, who had long been responsible for supervising the bank’s business in Italy. After they were promoted, both insisted they had known nothing of Santorini.
It is impossible to ask Jain or Broeksmit about the incident. Jain died of cancer in 2022 and Broeksmit hanged himself in his London villa in 2014, with questions still unanswered about his reasons for committing suicide. Fitschen has declined to comment.
And then there is an additional chapter in this financial thriller: Why were German financial oversight authorities initially critical of Sewing only to then reverse course and become surprisingly restrained?
BaFin, after all, raised early doubts about the restatement of the Santorini deal, with which Deutsche Bank had hoped to continue making large deals with limited capital investment. Frauke Menke, who was head of large bank supervision at BaFin at the time, was particularly skeptical.
She had had a sharp eye on the financial institution at least since Jain’s appointment as CEO. The affair surrounding the manipulation of the LIBOR interest rates, which Deutsche Bank had been involved in, the lack of true contrition for the many years of uncontrolled profligacy in the investment banking sector: Menke was not going to back down, and she occasionally sent the management board and Supervisory Board Chairman Achleitner caustic letters that would trigger panic on the bank’s top floors.
As she did in the Santorini case, as well. Menke initially demanded information on Santorini from the bank in April 2012, after even the U.S. Federal Reserve questioned the deal. Following a critical report published by the Bloomberg news agency, she complained in summer 2013 that the bank’s attempts at clarification had thus far been insufficient. Board members Krause and Leithner defended the accounting practices they had used to that point – only to notify BaFin one week later that it was redeclaring the Santorini deal as a derivative transaction.
Menke’s response was typical. The claim that allegedly new internal information made the restatement necessary was "completely implausible” and the bank’s behavior was "unacceptable.” Instead, she wrote, Santorini and similar deals were "a deliberate business strategy pursued by management.”
The dispute with BaFin culminated in the supervisory authority commissioning a special investigation of its own, the results of which, in late 2014, ended up putting Sewing in a particularly bad light. The "negligent, significant delay in the bank’s own investigation” of the Santorini deal was "a product of the bank’s defensive stance,” particularly that of the legal department, the report reads. A desire to clarify the matter "was not discernible for long stretches.” This "also applies to Internal Audit,” Sewing’s department.
From April 2012 to August 2013, the report notes, BaFin was provided "with several false statements” and no internal investigation of the Santorini deal was undertaken, despite this having been an imperative given the accusations and suspicions swirling in the regulatory agency and in the public at large. Responsibility, the report established, lay primarily with Leithner’s legal department, Krause’s finance department and Sewing’s internal auditing department.
But then came the about-face.
BaFin voiced surprisingly little criticism of the special investigation ultimately carried out by Sewing – a rather unexpected result given biting tone the supervisory authority had previously used in communications with Deutsche Bank. There were "no indications” that Sewing’s investigation had been "inadequate or hadn’t been independent,” aside from the apparently shoddy checks of the electronic communications surrounding the Santorini deal.
Menke, who still works at BaFin today, declined to discuss why she suddenly turned down the heat on Sewing all those years ago. Nor why BaFin, in late 2014, shortly after the presentation of its audit report, approved the promotion of Sewing to the board, effective January 2015, despite his questionable role in the investigation of the Santorini deal.
It could be that BaFin simply decided that the scandal surrounding the manipulated LIBOR rates, which Sewing had nothing to do with, was more important than the Santorini deal.
BaFin, which was then joined by the Deutsche Bank supervisory board, forced Jain to resign as CEO in summer 2015. He was succeeded by John Cryan, who then cut ties with Faissola, who Jain had put in charge of the bank’s gigantic asset management business. Finance head Krause and legal department boss Leithner also had to go. And Sewing’s rise through the bank’s upper echelons began.
These days, Krause and Leithner no longer have anything to do with the bank. Krause, who was once a member of the board at BMW, invested in electric cars and other projects, while Leithner is head of the Deutsche Börse Group. Faissola, though, hasn’t been able to leave Deutsche Bank behind, both because of Santorini and because he is an advisor to the Qatari’s ruling Al-Thani family, which has been the largest stakeholder in Deutsche Bank since 2014. For a time, his legal advisor in the LIBOR affair, Stefan Simon, was even a member of the Deutsche Bank board.
Faissola frequently tells confidants how unfairly he feels he has been treated and how deep the rift is between him and the bank. The Italian coordinates his activities and is preparing his lawsuit against Deutsche Bank from his office near Hyde Park in London. The value of that suit is likely to be significantly higher than the one filed by Schiraldi: For many years, Faissola was thought to be one of the top earners at Deutsche Bank.
And Sewing? He continued to climb the executive ladder. In 2015, he became head of private and corporate customers. In 2017, he was appointed to the deputy CEO position. He finally became CEO in 2018. And all those promotions were approved by BaFin, which had been so critical of his work as auditor.
Sewing is the only one involved in the Santorini deal who still works for Deutsche Bank. As CEO, he has gotten the bank back on track, pacified the relationship with the supervisory authorities and filled the supervisory and management boards with allies, to the point that there are hardly any critical voices at all anymore.
Now, though, the shadows of the past are catching up with him. And he will soon have to address them. In court.
